summary: A romance of joy and grief in which love, jealousy, and class contempt play out aboard a doomed ship, and fear and cold take fifteen hundred lives.

need-to-breathe.why: Rose and Jack are pulled under when the ship goes down, hundreds drown in the corridors and the freezing sea, and Rose must get her breath back before she can whistle.

hungry.why: First-class dinners are social set pieces; no one hungers.

sleepy.why: Rose dozes on the floating door as the cold takes her, and old Rose closes her eyes at the end, but sleep is barely a theme.

urge-to-cough.why: No cough is described; Jack's spitting lesson is sport, not reflex.

dizzy.why: Rose dangles over the stern rail, passengers slide down the tilting decks as the stern rises, and Rose reels at the steerage party.

fatigued.why: Jack and Rose fight through flooded corridors and climb the rising stern, and Rose, frozen and spent, forces herself off the door to swim for the whistle.

pain.why: Jack describes water so cold it hits like a thousand knives, Cal strikes Rose across the face, and a falling funnel crushes swimmers.

disgusted.why: Rose is revolted by the suffocating society she is sold into, and Ruth and Cal treat steerage, and Jack, as something unclean.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The sea is twenty-eight degrees; Jack freezes to death holding Rose's hand, and the fifteen hundred in the water die of cold within minutes.

afraid.why: Rose clings to the stern as the ship stands vertical, mothers in steerage are locked behind gates, and fifteen hundred people scream in the water.

anxious.why: Rose dreads the life Cal and her mother have planned, Ruth frets over the family's debts, and Andrews paces knowing there are not enough lifeboats.

panic.why: The crowd stampedes for the last boats, Murdoch fires into the mob, Tommy is shot, and Rose and Jack race rising water through the corridors.

sensory-pleasures.why: Rose drinks beer and dances in steerage, flies in the wind at the bow, and makes love with Jack in the Renault in the hold.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Rose hangs her Monet and Picasso in the stateroom, pores over Jack's Paris sketches, and asks him to draw her like one of his French girls.

fun-excitement.why: Jack wins his ticket at poker, teaches Rose to spit, and takes her to the steerage party for dancing, beer, and arm-wrestling.

orgasm.why: Rose and Jack make love in the back of the Renault, the handprint on the fogged window telling the rest.

love-romantic.why: Rose and Jack fall in love in three days aboard the ship, and the old Rose has carried him in her heart for eighty-four years.

love-family.why: Ruth tells Rose the family's survival depends on the match, Rose chooses Jack over her mother, and a steerage mother tells her children a bedtime story as the water rises.

grief.why: Rose weeps over Jack's frozen body and must pry his hand from hers, and old Rose grieves him still as she tells the story.

missing-someone.why: Old Rose has missed Jack for eighty-four years and has no picture of him; he exists now only in her memory.

aroused-sexually.why: Jack draws Rose nude wearing only the necklace, trembling at the sight, and the two give in to desire in the cargo hold.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Jack and Fabrizio win the trip together and Fabrizio dies under a funnel, and Molly Brown befriends Rose and lends Jack a tuxedo.

empathy.why: Jack sees the fire in Rose that her world will put out, and Rose, in the lifeboat, cannot bear to leave him and jumps back aboard.

compassion.why: Jack risks himself to talk Rose off the stern, Molly Brown pleads with the lifeboat to go back, and Officer Lowe rows into the dead to find survivors.

grateful.why: Cal thanks Jack for saving Rose with a dinner invitation and a tip, and Rose's gratitude turns to love.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Jack enjoys showing Rose how to live, but helping is love's expression, not its own pleasure.

trustful-distrustful.why: Jack asks Rose to trust him at the bow, Lovejoy slips the necklace into Jack's coat so Cal can brand him a thief, and Cal buys his way into a lifeboat with a crying child.

depressed.why: Rose, seeing nothing but a long parade of parties and no one who sees her, climbs over the stern rail to jump.

angry.why: Cal upends the breakfast table in fury, hunts Jack and Rose through the flooding ship with Lovejoy's pistol, and Rose spits in his face.

envious.why: Cal cannot bear that Rose prefers a penniless artist, but envy as such is faint.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Cal's jealousy of Jack drives him to frame Jack, slap Rose, and finally shoot at them both as the ship sinks.

jealous-friendship.why: There is no friendship rank at stake.

hatred.why: Cal comes to hate Jack as the man who took what was his, and Rose hates Cal enough to spit in his face and leave his name behind.

contempt.why: Ruth and Cal sneer at Jack's rootless life over dinner, steerage passengers are locked behind gates, and Cal calls Jack a gutter rat.

resentment.why: Rose resents being sold to Cal to pay her father's debts, and the steerage passengers rage at the locked gates that keep them from the boats.

proud.why: Ismay wants headlines and Smith his crowning voyage, Cal shows off the Heart of the Ocean, and the unsinkable ship is everyone's pride.

amused.why: Jack charms the dinner table with his life story, Molly Brown's wisecracks puncture the snobs, and Rose laughs learning to spit.

sense-of-belonging.why: Rose belongs to a first class she despises and finds her people at the steerage party, while Jack is tolerated at dinner as a curiosity.

lonely.why: Rose tells Jack she felt she was standing in a crowded room screaming and no one looked up.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Rose judges her mother and Cal for selling her, the film judges Ismay and the lifeboat shortage, and Murdoch shoots himself after killing a passenger.

admiration.why: Rose admires Jack's drawings and his freedom, and Andrews, Smith, and the band are admired for staying at their posts.

embarrassed.why: Jack arrives at dinner in Molly Brown's son's tuxedo and fumbles the forks, and Cal finds Rose's nude drawing in his safe.

shame.why: Ruth is terrified of the shame of being seen as poor, and Cal is humiliated when Rose chooses a steerage boy in front of him.

guilt.why: Andrews apologizes to Rose for not building a stronger ship, Murdoch shoots himself after killing a passenger, and the lifeboat crews feel the guilt of not going back.

sad.why: The sinking is told as grief: the Strauses in bed, the mother and her children, the band's last hymn, and Rose's whispered promise to Jack.

happy.why: Rose is happy for the first time with Jack on the bow and in steerage, and old Rose shows photos of a life lived as she promised.

joyful-euphoric.why: Jack shouts that he is king of the world from the bow, Rose flies with her arms out at sunset, and they whirl drunk through the steerage dance.

effort.why: Rose runs through flooding decks for the axe to free Jack, they climb the vertical stern, and Rose hauls herself onto the door and off it again for the whistle.

focused-in-flow.why: Jack sketches Rose in absorbed silence, and the band plays on without a flicker as the deck tilts.

bored.why: Rose sees her future as the same mindless chatter at the same narrow people, and is bored enough to die.

distracted.why: The lookouts, watching Jack and Rose kiss on deck, see the iceberg too late.

impatient.why: Rose chafes through dinners, and the officers rush the lifeboats as time runs out.

curious.why: Brock Lovett dives the wreck for the diamond and hears the whole story, and Rose questions Jack about Paris and the ten-cent sketches.

surprised.why: The lookouts are stunned by the iceberg, Jack is stunned when Rose leaps from the lifeboat back to the ship, and Lovett learns the diamond was in Rose's pocket all along.

awe.why: Passengers marvel at the ship of dreams, and later watch in horror and wonder as the stern lifts into the night sky before it falls.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Lovett's crew doubt the old woman's claim to be Rose, and Cal doubts Rose will defy him until she does.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Old Rose sees the drawing on television and knows it at once; the memory of eighty-four years comes back whole.

confused.why: Passengers wander the tilting decks unsure what is happening, and Rose is bewildered when the necklace turns up in Jack's coat.

frustrated.why: Rose cannot get anyone to help free Jack, steerage pounds on locked gates, and Cal cannot get a shot at the pair he hunts.

uncertain-certain.why: Rose decides, then undecides, between the lifeboat and Jack, and between her mother's plan and her own life.

understanding.why: Andrews calculates with certainty that the ship will founder in an hour or two, and Rose understands that Jack saved her in every way a person can be saved.

inspired.why: Jack sees that the stern will go last and gets them to it, Rose grabs a fire axe to free him, and takes the whistle from a dead officer.

satisfied.why: Old Rose drops the Heart of the Ocean into the sea with quiet satisfaction, her promise to Jack kept.

foreboding.why: Old Rose tells the story knowing the end, and Andrews warns of too few lifeboats before the iceberg is sighted.

nostalgia.why: The whole film is old Rose's memory of three days in 1912, the ship of dreams restored in her telling.

anticipation-suspense.why: The passengers wait for boats that are too few, and Rose waits on the door for a rescue that comes almost too late.

hope.why: Jack makes Rose promise to survive and have babies and die warm in her bed, and the dying wait in the water hoping the boats will come back.

schadenfreude.why: Rose enjoys spitting in Cal's face, and old Rose notes with some satisfaction that Cal shot himself in the crash of 1929.

elevation.why: The band plays Nearer My God to Thee, the Strauses stay together in bed, and Jack gives Rose the door and his life.

infatuation.why: Rose and Jack fall headlong in three days; old Rose admits it was the most erotic moment of her life.

rage.why: Cal, enraged, upends the breakfast table and later fires wildly at Jack and Rose down a flooding staircase.
